catalog_locator: Browne et al. 2024: p. 117, sec. 1 Introduction, left column, second paragraph; p. 119, sec. 3 results, paragraph before Figure 2 and the Table 2 discussion. Capell 1953: p. 299 (whole-issue scan p. 61; scan), paragraph headed 'Stress'.
catalog_quote: [Browne et al. 2024:117] Hale noted a general lengthening process of post-tonic consonants, which is only distinctive for stops (primary stress in Warumungu is generally word-initial; with secondary stress on non-word-final alternating syllables, with some lexical exceptions). This analysis was continued by Prithindra Chakravarti, who further observed a complementary distribution between long vowels and long consonants in stressed syllables, which he labelled “bimorism or bisyllabism” [7]. [...] [p. 119] MODE 1 stops are relatively unrestricted, able to occur in the onset of any syllable. MODE 2 stops are primarily found in disyllables following primary stress. [...] 89% of MODE 2 stops are found following a primary stress (i.e. 1 preceding syllable), the majority of which are found in disyllable words; and 7% following secondary stress (i.e. 3 preceding syllables). The remaining 4% of MODE 2 stops are found in the onset of the third syllable, e.g. /kuɭaɲcːari/ ‘diamond dove’. In addition to stress pattern restrictions, MODE 2 stops cannot follow long vowels [...] || [Capell 1953:299] Stress. Stress tends to fall on the penultimate of two-syllabled words, and the antepenultimate of longer words. Words of more than three syllables are not common, and mostly compounded. In this case there is a subsidiary stress on the initial syllable of the word. There is no particularly outstanding tonal pattern, and no attempt has been made in this sketch to deal with questions of tonality.

The remaining 4…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the first syllable of the word; secondary stresses fall on alternating syllables thereafter (3rd, 5th..), but not on a word-final syllable; a few lexical exceptions exist. Corroborated independently by Evans 1982 (snippet: 'the first syllable is stressed, then every second syllable after that'), Menning & Nash 1981 ('Stress is on the first syllable'), and, for 2-3-syllable words, by Capell 1953:299 ('penultimate of two-syllabled words, and the antepenultimate of longer words').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Alternating rhythmic secondary stress on non-final odd-numbered syllables (Browne et al. 2024). Evans 1982 (snippet) adds a morphological override: 'the first syllable of long suffixes always takes secondary stress: papulu-kkuna house-to'. Capell 1953 describes longer (mostly compounded) words as having a 'subsidiary stress on the initial syllable' with main stress antepenultimate, an older formulation at odds with the modern initial-primary analysis for 4+ syllable words.
new_statements.exceptions: Browne et al. 2024: 'with some lexical exceptions' (not itemised); 4% of long stops occur in third-syllable onsets (e.g. /kuɭaɲcːari/ 'diamond dove'), outside the post-tonic positions. Second-position pronouns are cliticised and their stress is subordinated to the preceding word (Mushin & Simpson 2008:585; Simpson 2008).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement (phonological word incl. suffixes); post-tonic consonant lengthening/long stops are tied to the primary-stressed initial syllable. The SST paper is an acoustic study of stops; the stress statement is given as descriptive background by a team including the language's principal describer (J. Simpson). The fuller first-hand treatments (Simpson 2002 learner's guide; Heath & Simpson 1982 sketch grammar; Evans 1982) were not accessible beyond snippets.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Warumungu proper (waru1265; Capell's 'Waramunga', Hale/Heath 'Warramunga' are older spellings of the same language, recorded at Phillip Creek/Tennant Creek). No dialect differentiation is reported for stress. Browne et al. 2024 use legacy recordings (Hale 1959, Chakravarti 1966, Heath 1977) plus recent fieldwork with Tennant Creek speakers.
